Dinner, Planned: 5 Minutes to Less Mental Load

Emily Oster, PhD

Jul. 28, 2026 4 minute read
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:18
Instaread

For many years, I sat down at the end of the week to plan the next week’s dinners, and got frustrated. I was trying to have variety (but not too much!), to make sure I thought about who was home on which day, to use up the random leftover beans that we somehow always had. Surely, I thought over and over again, there is a better way to do this. But I never found the right program or app to deliver what I wanted: something simple, but customizable.

Finally, I got fed up and I decided to build something myself. At first, I thought it was just for me – but a little user testing and a few iterations later, I decided others might find this useful too.

And thus was built: Dinner, Planned, from ParentData. It’s designed to take the planning off your (dinner) plate. You add recipes, you tell it who is home, and it builds a varied week (and a grocery list). In the simplest form, you can go from sign-up to a week of dinners in about 5 minutes – and if you want to get fancy, you can do that too.

The Five Minute Starting Plan

I’ve used meal apps before where the setup alone is several hours before I can even start doing anything. The goal here was to let you see how it works within five minutes. The fastest path is four steps:

  1. Log in with your ParentData account (the tool is included in your paid subscription, and part of a free trial)
  2. Load the starter recipe pack so you’ve got something to work with (also, these recipes are great, simple, and a lot are kid-friendly)
  3. Hit “Plan Week”, then hit “Suggest” – It will fill the week for you. If you don’t like something, you can ask it to re-suggest that day. When you’re happy, click “commit”.
  4. Week done. The grocery list auto populates by store location, and lets you add any extras you need.

When you go to cook, you can view your recipes right in the program (this spinach pasta: surprisingly successful with children).

Adding Recipes

The biggest value, but also the biggest pain, in any meal planning is adding recipes. I’ve tried to make that as easy as possible – we’ve got a million ways to add them. Including…

  • Upload a scanned photo or PDF – the computer reads it and formats it for you (yes, including your grandmother’s handwritten recipes)
  • Upload a CSV or a file outputted from another recipe app – it will read almost any format
  • Copy and paste, or enter by hand
  • Have other friends on the platform? Ask them to share. Share packs let you send your recipes to others with a simple code (try FA7J3Q to get some of my family’s favorites…)

Once you’ve got these recipes in, you can tag them (vegetarian, easy to make, slow cooker, etc). Then you’re ready to get fancy.

Ready to get Fancy?

When I was developing this, I worked with a bunch of users to test it, and together we built in a lot of really cool functionality to help you make this your own. Some examples:

  • You can mark your recipes as a no-go for certain people (got a kid who doesn’t eat chicken? Me too). Tell the tool who is there for dinner that night, and it will avoid suggesting things they won’t eat.
  • Flag ingredients to use up this week – the computer will pick meals that use them.
  • Use recipe tags liberally – you can request vegetarian on Monday, a slow cooker meal on Thursday, or tell the tool to snooze a tag for a while. So you never get soup in the summer.
  • When everyone loves something, make it a “Favorite” and it will come up more often.

Try it

There is no substitute for trying this out – so I hope you do. The link is below – you’re automatically in if you’re a ParentData subscriber, and this is all there as part of our two-week free trial. Which is plenty of time to get started. If you’ve got questions or suggestions, just email us: ask@parentdata.org.
